title: Trump acquitted without trial

stances.claim: The US Senate's 52-48 and 53-47 acquittal of Donald Trump on Feb 5, 2020 was 'unabashedly partisan' -- conducted without trial, without testimonial evidence, and without documentary evidence -- and the preceding 51-49 vote on Jan 31 barring oral and testimonial evidence (with only Romney and Collins crossing over) made the partisan acquittal inevitable.
stances.rhetorical_move: vote-tabulation analysis exposing the partisan structure beneath the ceremonial processes

stances.claim: The Republican legal argument -- that 'abuse of power' and 'obstruction of the House' fall outside the US Constitution's enumerated grounds of 'treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors' because they are not 'criminal acts' -- represents a verbal-legis / literal interpretation (as contradistinguished from a liberal one) that, applied for 250 years, explains why no US president has ever been ousted by the Senate.
stances.rhetorical_move: literal-vs-liberal interpretive characterization to frame the doctrinal source of Senate-trial outcomes

stances.claim: The framers of the 1987 Philippine Constitution provided 'more encompassing' impeachment grounds -- including the catch-all 'betrayal of public trust' alongside 'culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes' -- precisely so that abuses of power could not be textually dumped the way Republicans dumped the Trump charges.
stances.rhetorical_move: Filipino-framers-anticipated-this-problem framing to credit the 1987 Charter's drafters

stances.claim: The Philippine impeachment record bears out the constitutional difference: Estrada's trial was truncated by House prosecutors' walkout (precipitating the Edsa II People Power Revolution), but the Corona impeachment proceeded for several months without testimonial blockade, included testimony from former Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales and Corona himself, and culminated in a more-than-three-fourths Senate vote 'without any unabashedly partisan alignment' -- making the Philippine process fairer, more democratic, and less partisan than its US counterpart.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparative case study (Estrada + Corona) as empirical evidence for the comparative-doctrine claim

stances.claim: Beyond the broader grounds, the Philippine guilty-judgment threshold is more than three-fourths of the Senate, while the US threshold is only two-thirds -- a structural reinforcement that further raises the legitimacy bar for an ouster verdict.
stances.rhetorical_move: threshold-comparison reinforcement of the constitutional-fairness claim

notable_anecdotes: The five ceremonial Senate processes that produced no substantive trial -- (1) oath of 'impartial justice,' (2) listening to oral arguments, (3) written questions submitted to CJ John Roberts who read them aloud, (4) answers from managers and defense lawyers, (5) latitude for Democratic senators in questioning -- used by CJ as the carapace of judicial form around a 'plainly numerical' partisan outcome.

The Romney-Collins crossover on the Jan 31 evidence-barring vote (51-49) and Romney's lone Article-1 conviction vote -- used to underline how slender the bipartisanship became and how thoroughly the 53-45 GOP-Dem split otherwise held.

The Edsa II People Power Revolution as the contingent eruption when House prosecutors walked out of Estrada's truncated trial -- a flagship instance of impeachment-process failure converting into street power, with CJ implicitly contrasting that to the rule-of-law completion of Corona's later trial.

Corona's trial inclusion of Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales and Corona himself as witnesses, contrasted with Trump's Senate denying any witness testimony at all -- a sharp empirical illustration of the doctrinal-process gap.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban reports the Feb 5, 2020 US Senate acquittal of President Donald Trump as 'an unabashedly partisan vote' -- without trial, without testimonial evidence, and without documentary evidence -- with all 53 Republicans voting to dismiss Article 2 (obstruction of House investigation) 53-47, and all 53 Republicans except Mitt Romney voting to dismiss Article 1 (abuse of power for withholding ~$400M in military aid to Ukraine unless Joe Biden was investigated) 52-48. The preceding 51-49 vote on Jan 31 barring oral and testimonial evidence (with Romney and Susan Collins crossing) made the partisan outcome inevitable. The five ceremonial Senate processes -- oath of 'impartial justice,' oral arguments, written questions read aloud by CJ John Roberts, manager/defense replies, and latitude for Democratic questioners -- formed the carapace of judicial form around a plainly numerical outcome. Republicans argued that 'abuse of power' and 'obstruction' fall outside the US Constitution's enumerated grounds ('treason, bribery, or other high crimes and misdemeanors') because they are not 'criminal acts' -- a verbal-legis literal interpretation that, in 250 years, has produced no Senate-ousted US president (Andrew Johnson 1868, Clinton 1999, and Trump all acquitted; Nixon resigned). The 1987 Philippine Charter's framers, aware of this literal exclusion, provided 'more encompassing' grounds -- 'culpable violation of the Constitution, treason, bribery, graft and corruption, other high crimes and betrayal of public trust' -- so that abuses cannot be textually dumped. The catch-all 'betrayal of public trust' (plus the SALN Law) was partly used in both the Estrada and Corona impeachments. Estrada's trial was truncated by House prosecutors' walkout, precipitating the Edsa II People Power Revolution, but Corona's ran for several months without testimonial blockade -- including testimony from Ombudsman Conchita Carpio Morales and Corona himself -- and ended in a more-than-three-fourths Senate vote 'without any unabashedly partisan alignment.' The Philippine 3/4 threshold (vs the US 2/3) is also structurally higher. CJ concludes that the Philippine impeachment process, though also sui generis, is 'fairer, more democratic and less partisan' than its US counterpart.
